scenes.heading: Iteration and approximation with algorithms
scenes.sub: Guess, improve, repeat — until it is good enough
scenes.say: How does a calculator find the square root of ten? It does not know the answer. It starts with a guess and improves it again and again. That is iteration, and today you will learn to use it to model change and solve equations.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Too cold? Turn the shower a little hotter, then check again
scenes.science: Each new value comes from the last one using the same rule
scenes.breaks: You can feel the water. An algorithm blindly applies its rule, and some rules swing further from the answer every time.
scenes.say: Think of adjusting a shower. Too cold, turn it a bit hotter, check again. Each change is based on the last result. Iteration is the same: feed each answer back into the rule. But unlike you, an algorithm cannot feel the water, and some rules make things worse every time.

scenes.heading: A recurrence rule
scenes.question: uₙ₊₁ = 1.1uₙ − 50, u₀ = 1000. Find u₃.
scenes.say: A lake starts with a thousand fish. Each year they grow by ten percent, then fifty are caught. One point one times a thousand, minus fifty, is one thousand and fifty. Feed that back in: eleven hundred and five. Once more: eleven hundred and sixty-five point five.
scenes.caption: u₁ = 1.1 × 1000 − 50 = 1050. Feed it back in: u₂ = 1105. Once more: u₃ = 1165.5.

scenes.heading: Square roots by averaging
scenes.say: To find the square root of ten, start with a rectangle of area ten: two by five. Average the sides to get three point five, and the other side becomes about two point eight six. Again: about three point one eight by three point one five. It is nearly a square, and its side is the square root of ten.
scenes.caption: Start with a 2 by 5 rectangle of area 10. Average the sides: 3.5 by about 2.86. Again: about 3.18 by 3.15. Nearly a square — its side is √10.

scenes.heading: Solving x = √(x + 3)
notes: Up to the curve, across to y = x
scenes.say: To solve x squared minus x minus three equals zero, rearrange to x equals the square root of x plus three. First the curve and the line y equals x. Now the staircase: up to the curve, across to the line, up again. The steps shrink towards the crossing point, at about two point three zero.
scenes.caption: Solve x² − x − 3 = 0 as x = √(x + 3). Draw the curve and y = x. The staircase goes up to the curve, across to the line, up again, shrinking towards x ≈ 2.30.

scenes.heading: The stopping rule
steps: Apply the rule to get the next value
Compare it with the last value
Stop when both round the same
scenes.say: Iteration never lands exactly on the answer, so you need a stopping rule. Choose a start, apply the rule, and compare the new value with the last one. Stop when two in a row round to the same answer.

scenes.heading: When iteration fails
scenes.say: Careful: not every rearrangement works. The same equation written as x equals x squared minus three, starting at two, gives one, negative two, one, negative two, forever. That iteration diverges, so try a different rearrangement.
scenes.caption: Not every rearrangement works. x = x² − 3 from 2 gives 1, −2, 1, −2, forever. It diverges, so try another rearrangement.

points: Iterate: feed each output back in
Babylonian: average x and N ÷ x
Rearrange to x = g(x), then iterate
Stop when two in a row agree
scenes.say: Quick recap. Iteration feeds each answer back into the rule. Average x and N over x to find square roots. Rearrange equations into x equals g of x, but check the values settle. Stop when two in a row agree. Now try the practice questions!
